title: What You've Missed in Creator Bootcamp | Karat Blog
summary: Key takeaways from Creator Bootcamp: pitching brands, managing partnerships, and growing your business from top experts.
body_text: Creator Bootcamp Learnings So Far In case you missed the first half of Creator Bootcamp, here’s a quick recap of what we’ve learned so far: 1️⃣ Day 1: Keynote feat. Zack Honarvar (Pitching Brands) Who is Zack? Manager to Airrack and Yes Theory Co-founder of Creator Now and Fan of a Fan Our 3 Biggest Takeaways You need to find the right brand profile to pitch successfully. For early stage creators, Zack says the best opportunities come from companies that generate $1M to $10M in annual revenue (or have 10-100 employees) and make consumer packaged goods. Get creative on how you pitch. Attach a Loom video about why a brand should work with you or send a handwritten letter. Over-deliver on value—give a white glove experience. 2️⃣ Day 2: Making More Money with Lindsey Lugrin, Clayton Jacobs, and Grace Lemire Who are these people? Lindsey Lugrin → Founder of F*** You Pay Me , a brand deal database Clayton Jacobs → Founder of CreatorDB , an influencer marketing platform Grace Lemire → (me, the girl writing this ) content creator and freelance marketer Our 3 Biggest Takeaways Consider getting a manager. They can leverage their networks to increase your brand deal income. Just do your due diligence in choosing the right manager (they’re not all the same). If you want to land more brand deals, engage with them regularly on socials before you even pitch them. There are real people behind the accounts who will remember your name. If you complete one deal and the brand wants to work with you again, take the deal. Seeing that you’ve worked with another brand multiple times is a great signal to new brands. 3️⃣ Day 3: Scaling Your Content Business with Kristoph Oedman Who is Kristoph? Former President and Co-founder of video game coaching platform ProGuides (later got acquired) Scaled 10+ YouTube channels to a total 5M+ subscribers Our 3 Biggest Takeaways If you want to scale your content business, promise your audience one thing and commit to delivering that promise. Your community is your lifeblood. Engage with your community regularly. Make sure they feel heard. Scaling requires loyalty. How do you build that? By being consistent. 4️⃣ Day 4: Growing Your Community and Mastering Merch with Will Baumann and Hassan Khadair Who Are Will and Hassan? Will → Co-founder and CEO of Fourthwall , a platform for creators to quickly set up their own virtual shops Hassan → Comedian, creator, and puppet master who launched hiw own Steamboat Willie puppet with Fourthwall Our 3 Biggest Takeaways Custom products are better because they’re more differentiated. The downside is they take a lot more time and money to produce. If you’re able to move anywhere from 200-1,000 units of merch, you have a solid chance of being able to sell a custom product. Follower count isn’t an indicator of how well your product will sell—engagement is. Create a genuine relationship with your audience and your product will sell. 5️⃣ Day 5: Building Personal Brands with Qetsiyah Jacobson Who is Qetsiyah? Founder of Unserious , a community for the chronically online Creator Paid Partnerships Manager at Stan Our 3 Biggest Takeaways Get to know yourself. Qetsiyah recommends two exercises: List out everything about yourself (location, job, hobbies, etc.). Lean on these points in your content; don’t try to be somebody else. List out aspiring points vs. relatable points. Know what makes you relatable to the average person and what makes you stand out to the average person. Don’t do content pillars. Share your opinions (ie. controversial takes) and repeat. Set boundaries for yourself. Building a personal brand doesn’t mean putting everything out there. Decide what you want to keep private. What to Expect for the Rest of Creator Bootcamp Here’s what we have in store the rest of this week [ view full details here ]: Today: Internet Shaquille on launching great products Wednesday: A panel of tax experts on creator taxes 101 Thursday: Justin Moore from Creator Wizard on how to land better brand partnerships Friday: Hannah Dam from Healthy Gamer and LonnieIIV on avoiding burnout All sessions are at 1 PM PT // 4 PM ET in the Discord. Join here!

title: Oak Valley Community Bank Announces Commercial Banking Officer Hiring
summary: Oak Valley Community Bank Welcomes Pete Centeno as Vice President, Branch Manager of Ripon Branch.
body_text: OAKDALE, CA – Oak Valley Community Bank, a wholly-owned subsidiary of Oak Valley Bancorp (NASDAQ: OVLY), is pleased to announce that Joel Burns has joined the Bank as Vice President, Commercial Banking Officer. Based at the Bank's Lodi Branch, located at 31 South School Street, Burns will serve commercial and agricultural clients throughout the Lodi market. Burns brings 25 years of commercial banking experience, with extensive expertise in relationship management and business lending. Most recently, he served as a Commercial Banker at another local financial institution. In his new role, he will focus on commercial and agricultural lending, working closely with business owners to understand their goals and deliver customized financial solutions that support their long-term success. “Joel brings a strong background in commercial banking, with a focus on building lasting client relationships and delivering thoughtful credit solutions for agricultural businesses,” said Gary Stephens, Executive Vice President, Commercial Banking Group. “His collaborative approach and commitment to understanding each client's unique needs help foster the trusted partnerships that are at the heart of our relationship-based banking philosophy.” Burns earned a Bachelor of Science in Agribusiness from California Polytechnic State University, San Luis Obispo, and is a graduate of the Southwestern Graduate School of Banking at Southern Methodist University. He is actively involved with the Lodi District Grape Growers Association. Outside of work, he enjoys spending time with family and friends. Oak Valley Bancorp operates Oak Valley Community Bank & their Eastern Sierra Community Bank division, through which it offers a variety of loan and deposit products to individuals and small businesses. They currently operate through 19 conveniently located branches: Oakdale, Turlock, Stockton, Patterson, Ripon, Escalon, Manteca, Tracy, Sacramento, Roseville, Lodi, two branches in Sonora, three branches in Modesto, and three branches in the Eastern Sierra division which includes Bridgeport, Mammoth Lakes, and Bishop. title: BAT recognised with triple win at the 2026 Red Dot Awards
summary: BAT's design capability has been recognised with three Red Dots for glo Hilo Plus, Vuse Pro One Box and Vuse Ultra x McLaren.
body_text: glo Hilo Plus, Vuse Pro One Box and Vuse Ultra x McLaren have been recognised for excellence in product design in the Red Dot Award: Product Design 2026. The awards highlight BAT's growing design capability and commitment to creating products that combine innovation, functionality and user-centred thinking. The Red Dot Awards are among the most respected honours in the global design industry, celebrating products that excel in innovation, functionality, usability and design quality. While the awards recognise three individual products, they also represent something bigger – the evolution of design as a core capability within BAT. Today, BAT’s in-house design function spans industrial design, user experience, and sustainability, helping shape products across our portfolio. Recognition from the world's leading design professionals Every year, thousands of products from around the world are assessed by independent juries comprising experienced design professionals, who evaluate entries against criteria including innovation, usability, functionality and design excellence. For BAT, participation in these awards is about more than recognition. It provides an opportunity to benchmark products against leading global brands and gain independent feedback from experts at the forefront of the design industry. The awards also demonstrate the importance of design in creating products that resonate with adult nicotine consumers. glo Hilo Plus Vuse Ultra x McLaren Vuse Pro One Box More than aesthetics Design awards are often associated with how products look, but Red Dot judges evaluate much more than appearance. Products are assessed on how effectively they work, how intuitive they are to use, and how successfully they improve the overall user experience. That philosophy mirrors BAT's own approach to product design. Every aspect of the consumer experience – from ergonomics and usability to product features and interface design – is considered throughout the development process. The results are products that combine technology, functionality and design in ways that meet the evolving expectations of adult nicotine consumers. Designing for the future The three award-winning products are the result of collaboration across design, research and development, engineering and commercial teams. Together, they demonstrate how thoughtful design can elevate product experiences and deliver internationally recognised innovation. As we continue to develop our Smokeless products, design remains central to how we translate consumer insights and technology into intuitive, functional and distinctive experiences for adult nicotine consumers. Information about the Red Dot Award: Product Design 2026 The Red Dot Award: Product Design is one of the internationally established competitions for product design. Since 1955, it has recognised products that stand out for their high design quality. At the core of the competition is the thorough evaluation by the independent Red Dot Jury. It examines all submissions in detail and discusses them regarding key aspects of good design – including function, usability, responsibility and aesthetic quality. The jury is composed of internationally experienced experts from various disciplines. Submissions come from numerous countries and are assessed through a multi-stage evaluation process.

title: Accounting Automation Myths That Keep Finance Teams Stuck in Manual Work
summary: Discover how accounting automation myths mislead finance teams into manual work. Learn to streamline workflows and preserve unique client needs.
body_text: Your close doesn't break because AI missed a magic answer; it breaks when prepared work can't be traced back to source. That's where the accounting automation myths that sound reassuring in a sales deck start to cost the team time. A CAS practice can standardize checklists across clients, but each client still brings different mappings, reviewer notes, and close habits into the workpaper. The useful question is simple: can the workflow prepare the work your reviewer already knows how to inspect? Recurring accounting work is not generic. Two CAS clients can run the same donation reconciliation, processor settlement, or accrual schedule and still use different mappings, cutoffs, dimensions, exceptions, and review conventions. If the workflow can't preserve that logic, the output may look finished while the reviewer still has to rebuild the work by hand. Key Takeaways: Accounting automation myths usually fail because they confuse output with reviewable work. Generic templates break when client-specific mappings, cutoffs, and classifications matter. The workpaper is the right review surface because it ties source, calculation, treatment, exceptions, and sign-off together. CAS practices need repeatable workflows that preserve each client's rules without creating a bespoke process for every account. The accountant stays in the loop. AI prepares the work, routes exceptions, and waits for review before anything reaches the GL. Sage Intacct and QuickBooks Online should remain the system of record while preparation happens upstream. Why Accounting Automation Myths Break Reviewer Trust Accounting automation myths break reviewer trust when they promise finished answers without showing the preparation path. A reviewer needs source files, calculations, accounting treatment, exceptions, and sign-off in one place. Without that surface, automation just moves the rework from preparation to review. Clean Output Can Still Be Unreviewable A clean reconciliation is not the same as a reviewable reconciliation. You can have totals that tie, neat formatting, and a journal-entry draft that looks ready, while the reviewer still has no idea whether the processor fees were netted correctly or whether a grant restriction was carried into the right fund. That is where many accounting automation myths that sound plausible start to fail. They sell the appearance of completion. Picture a CAS manager reviewing a nonprofit client close at 6:30 p.m. The bank feed is current, the donor export is in a spreadsheet, and the processor report has a fee column that changed from last month. One preparer used the prior workpaper, another copied a mapping from a different client, and the reviewer now has to decide whether the variance is real or just a format problem. The work is not glamorous, but it is the work. To be fair, manual review exists for a reason. Accountants don't trust work because it is fast; they trust work because it can be traced, challenged, corrected, and signed off. The mistake is assuming manual touch is the only way to get that control. If the source, calculation, treatment, and exception path are visible, the reviewer can inspect the work without re-performing every clerical step. If that review surface is the gap you're trying to close, See Truewind in action inside the workflow where preparation meets review. Generic Templates Fail on Client Reality The useful unit of accounting automation is not the task name. It is the team's treatment of that task. A brokerage rollforward, a donation reconciliation, or an accrual schedule may look standard from a distance, but the actual work depends on account mappings, cutoffs, classifications, entity rules, and reviewer conventions that live in prior workpapers and staff memory. CAS practices feel this first because they serve many clients at once. One client codes processor fees to a program dimension. Another splits the same fees across departments. A third has a donor platform export with campaign names that don't match the GL dimensions. A rigid workflow can force those clients into one template, and a fully bespoke process can preserve every rule, but neither scales well across a practice. A better operating layer has to do something more specific: preserve client rules while producing consistent review artifacts. The reviewer should not have to ask, "Whose logic did the system use?" The workpaper should answer that question before the reviewer asks it. The Real Risk Is the Clean-Looking Wrong Path Controllers are not mainly afraid of obviously bad AI output. In practice, the scarier problem is clean-looking work that hides the path from source to conclusion. You can reject a bad answer quickly. You can't safely approve a polished reconciliation if you don't know how it was assembled. That is why the accounting automation myths that focus only on speed feel incomplete. Speed matters. Nobody wants staff spending days normalizing exports and retyping statement activity. Still, the close does not get better if the reviewer has to slow down later because the output lacks support, exception notes, and visible logic. The analogy I keep coming back to is the review binder. A good binder was never valuable because it was paper. It was valuable because the reviewer could move from source to schedule to journal entry without guessing which decision happened where. AI-prepared work has to recreate that property, not just produce a prettier answer. How to Separate Accounting Automation Myths From Workflow Reality The way to separate accounting automation myths from workflow reality is to test whether the system prepares work in the same review pattern your team already uses. If it can't learn prior treatment, show exceptions, and produce a traceable workpaper, it is not close automation. It is another input to review. Start With the Workpaper, Not the Prompt The fastest diagnostic is simple: ask what artifact the reviewer receives. If the answer is a paragraph, a chat response, or a spreadsheet with numbers but no treatment trail, the workflow is not ready for recurring close work. A workpaper is source, calculation, accounting treatment, exceptions, and reviewer sign-off in one place, in that order. Miss one piece and the reviewer has to fill the gap. Before approving any accounting automation workflow, check five things. Does the output show the source file behind each material line? Does it show how the number was calculated? Does it identify the accounting treatment applied? Does it separate exceptions from ordinary activity? Does it capture who reviewed, corrected, and approved the result? If the system can't answer those questions, the risk is not that AI is too bold. The risk is that the reviewer can't see enough. A generic prompt can still be useful for explanation, drafting, or research. That concession matters because not every finance use case needs a controlled workflow. Month-end preparation does. Once the output feeds a reconciliation, schedule, or journal entry, the reviewer needs an artifact they can inspect, not an answer they have to interrogate. Use Prior Periods as the Test Set Prior-period workpapers are the cleanest way to test whether accounting automation is real. Take a completed workflow from last month, provide the same source files and ERP balances, and ask the system to prepare the known result. Then compare the prepared output to the reviewed workpaper and examine the differences. Not just the final number. The path. The test should be specific. For a donation reconciliation, compare bank deposits, donor platform totals, processor fees, fund restrictions, campaign coding, and any timing differences. For a family-office brokerage workflow, compare dividends, interest, realized activity, fees, transfers, entity treatment, and rollforward balances. For a CAS practice, compare how the same workflow behaves across two clients with different rules. The goal is not to prove the system is perfect. The goal is to see whether it can reproduce the known process and expose where it differs. One customer phrase captures the practitioner standard better than any abstract claim: "Categorization is accurate, and we stopped having to double-check everything." Read carefully, though. The important part is not blind trust. The important part is that review effort moves from checking every routine item to inspecting the places that need judgment. Treat Exceptions as a Feature of the Workflow An exception queue is not a sign the workflow failed. It is often the sign the workflow understood its boundary. Missing statements, unexpected balance changes, mixed personal and business activity, and inconsistent classifications should not be smoothed over because they interrupt a clean report. They belong in front of an accountant. Set a rule for recurring workflows: if the item changes the accounting treatment, source completeness, entity boundary, or reviewer convention, it should surface as an exception. If it is ordinary activity that follows the learned process, it can be prepared for review. That split is where capacity comes from. The accountant does not leave the loop; the accountant stops spending the first pass on items that already follow the known rule. This is especially important for CAS firms because client reality changes. A donor platform adds a field. A processor report changes columns. A custodian statement arrives with a new footnote format. If the workflow pretends all of that is normal, reviewer trust breaks. If the workflow flags what changed and shows the source, the reviewer can make a call without starting from a blank spreadsheet. Preserve Client Rules Without Freezing the Firm A CAS practice needs consistency at the review artifact level, not sameness at the accounting treatment level. That distinction is easy to miss. The firm wants every client workflow to produce a readable reconciliation, support schedule, reviewer note trail, and journal-entry draft. The firm does not want every client forced into the same chart mapping, allocation rule, or cutoff convention. A useful test is to choose one recurring workflow across three clients and ask what must be standard. The format of the workpaper should be standard, the source trace should be standard, the exception queue should be standard, and the sign-off pattern should be standard. The mappings, dimensions, allocations, and cutoff rules may differ by client, and the workflow should preserve those differences instead of hiding them. That is where the old spreadsheet model had one real advantage: it let teams adapt. We should admit that. Spreadsheets are flexible, familiar, and easy to change when a client has an odd case. The cost is that the logic often lives in formulas, tabs, emails, and one senior person's memory. For firms trying to make client-specific logic inspectable without rebuilding the same close from scratch, Book a Truewind demo after you map the recurring workflow you want to standardize first. Keep the GL as the System of Record Sage Intacct and QuickBooks Online should remain the source of truth. The accounting automation myths that position AI as a new ledger misunderstand how controllers actually operate. The GL owns the posted books, reporting structure, financial statements, and downstream analysis. The preparation layer should sit upstream, where source files become workpapers and approved entries. The operating model is straightforward. Source files come in from banks, processors, donor platforms, custodians, payroll registers, and prior workpapers. The preparation workflow structures those inputs, applies learned accounting logic, prepares reconciliations and schedules, and routes exceptions to the reviewer. After sign-off, the approved output moves into the GL. Keep that boundary clear and the team knows who owns each decision. If a vendor says the system posts autonomously, ask what happens when the reviewer disagrees with the accounting treatment. If the answer is vague, stop there. The goal is not to move decision-making away from accountants. The goal is to move clerical assembly out of the way so judgment can begin earlier. How Truewind Prepares Reviewable Accounting Work Truewind prepares reviewable accounting work by sitting between source files and the GL, not by replacing either one. It ingests recurring inputs, applies the team's learned accounting logic, prepares workpapers and reconciliations, surfaces exceptions, and waits for reviewer sign-off before approved output moves downstream. Source Files Become Workpapers, Not Loose Extracts Truewind starts with the materials finance teams already receive: bank activity, credit-card statements, processor exports, donor-platform files, custodian brokerage statements, capital statements, payroll registers, prior workpapers, and operational exports. The point is not extraction by itself. The point is to structure those inputs into a workflow that feeds coding, reconciliation, schedule creation, exception review, and workpaper preparation. That matters because the hardest accounting automation myths that teams encounter usually treat source files as a preprocessing nuisance. In real close work, source files are the evidence. A donor export has campaign and restriction context. A processor report has fee and settlement detail. A custodian statement carries activity that has to respect entity treatment. Truewind keeps that source context attached to the prepared work so the reviewer can trace the line back to the file. Truewind also learns from historical examples, including prior workpapers, prior treatment, reviewer corrections, and confirmed classifications. That does not mean the system invents accounting policy. It means the next period starts from the team's known process rather than a generic default. A customer described the practical effect plainly: "Truewind automates a huge chunk of that busywork." The valuable word in that sentence is busywork, because the accountant still owns the accounting call. Exceptions Stay With the Accountant Truewind's review workflow is built around the idea that exceptions should be visible. Prepared workpapers, reconciliations, schedules, and journal-entry drafts sit alongside source links and exception queues. Accountants confirm, adjust, or send items back to preparation, and those decisions are captured against the workflow for later periods. That is the difference between controlled close automation and open-ended autonomy. Multi-source reconciliation can match activity across a donor platform, processor, and bank, or across a custodian, an investment-vehicle statement, and an ERP balance. Proactive anomaly detection can identify missing statements, unexpected balance changes, mixed activity, or inconsistent classifications. Human-in-the-loop review keeps the accountant in control of what gets accepted. The GL boundary stays intact. Truewind connects prepared output to Sage Intacct and QuickBooks Online, the documented systems of record, after reviewer confirmation. Coding, dimensions, and source references are preserved on the push. Nothing in that pattern asks the accountant to trust a black box, and nothing asks the finance team to replace the ledger that already owns the books. A few customer comments are worth reading as examples, not universal promises. One said, "If I had to describe Truewind in one word: Lifechanging." Another said, "It's not just about making bookkeeping simpler; it's about freeing up teams, and helping them focus on higher-value projects." A third put it more broadly: "It's like having an entire accounting department at our fingertips - efficient, accurate, and effortless." The common thread is not that accountants disappear. The common thread is that preparation stops consuming the whole close. If that is the operating model you want to inspect against your own workpapers, Get a Truewind demo after you choose one recurring workflow with enough prior-period examples to test. What Controllers Should Automate Next Controllers should automate the recurring preparation work that has clear prior examples, reviewer ownership, and repeatable source files. Start where the team already has evidence of the right answer. The best first workflow is not the flashiest one; it is the one your reviewer can compare against last period. Pick a reconciliation, rollforward, or schedule that repeats every month and already has a known review pattern. Donation and processor reconciliations work well when donor exports, payout reports, bank activity, and fund coding repeat. Brokerage and capital statement workflows work when entity rules and prior workpapers are available. CAS client workflows work when the firm can standardize the review artifact while preserving each client's mappings and dimensions. The accounting automation myths that deserve to go away are the ones that flatten this work into data entry or pretend the accountant should leave the loop. Real preparation is source, logic, exception, and sign-off. What goes away is not the accountant. What goes away is the pile of clerical assembly that used to happen before the accountant could use judgment. Frequently Asked Questions How do I handle edge cases effectively? To handle edge cases effectively, start by defining clear rules for exceptions in your workflow. Use Truewind's proactive anomaly detection to identify discrepancies like missing statements or unexpected balance changes. This feature helps surface items that need your judgment instead of hiding them. Once identified, review these exceptions carefully, ensuring that you understand the context and source before making any decisions. Document your findings and adjust your processes as needed to improve future handling of similar cases. What if my source documents are inconsistent? If your source documents are inconsistent, Truewind can help by automatically ingesting and structuring these materials. Upload your raw financial data, such as bank statements and credit card activity, into Truewind. The platform organizes this data into a structured workflow, making it easier to reconcile and prepare for review. This reduces the manual effort of normalizing documents and allows your team to focus on the actual accounting work rather than formatting issues. Can I automate my recurring accounting tasks? Yes, you can automate your recurring accounting tasks with Truewind. Start by identifying the workflows that repeat each month, like reconciliations or journal entries. Once you've mapped out these processes, Truewind can ingest the necessary source documents and apply your team's established rules for transaction coding. This way, you can automate the preparation of workpapers and schedules, freeing up your team to focus on higher-value tasks while maintaining control over the review process. When should I review prepared workpapers? You should review prepared workpapers before any output is posted to the general ledger. Truewind's human-in-the-loop review workflow allows you to inspect reconciliations, schedules, and journal-entry drafts alongside their source documents. This ensures that you can trace each entry back to its origin and confirm the accuracy of the work. Regular reviews help maintain trust in the automation process and ensure that all exceptions are addressed before finalizing entries. Why does my team need to maintain control over the accounting process? Your team needs to maintain control over the accounting process to ensure accuracy and accountability. Truewind enhances this control by automating repetitive tasks while keeping the human review component intact. This means that while Truewind prepares the work, your team can focus on judgment calls and exceptions that require deeper analysis. By preserving the review process, you can trust that the outputs are reliable and that any discrepancies are addressed before they affect your financial reporting.

title: The best B2B data providers in 2026
summary: The 10 best B2B data providers and enrichment tools in 2026, compared on coverage, accuracy, compliance, and pricing, with honest verdicts for each.
body_text: Artisan is the best B2B data provider for teams that want data and activation in one system: waterfall enrichment across roughly a dozen providers, a database of over 250 million B2B professionals in over 200 countries, Artisan Local Data with over 250 million local businesses, and an AI business development representative (BDR) who puts the data to work. ZoomInfo wins on enterprise US depth, Cognism on EMEA compliance, and Apollo on price-performance. This guide was updated July 2026, with pricing checked as of that date. Comparison table: The top B2B data providers at a glance Provider Best for Standout capability Public pricing 1. Artisan Data plus activation in one platform Over 250 million B2B professionals and over 250 million local businesses, with waterfall enrichment feeding an AI BDR Hybrid: usage-based credits for Ava's work, dialer seats billed separately, free trial ( pricing ) 2. ZoomInfo Enterprise US depth Over 321 million profiles, over 70 million direct dials (vendor figures), org charts From around $15K a year, quote-based 3. Apollo Price-performance Over 230 million contacts inside an all-in-one engagement platform Free to $119/user/month 4. Cognism EMEA coverage and compliance Diamond Data phone-verified mobiles, DNC scrubbing Quote-based (around $15K to $50K a year reported) 5. Clay DIY waterfall orchestration Over 150 enrichment providers in one workflow builder Launch from $167 a month, Growth from $446 a month, plus free tier 6. People Data Labs Developers and data teams API-first access to over 3 billion person records (vendor figure) Free 100 lookups; Pro from $98 a month 7. UpLead Small-business accuracy on a budget 95% accuracy guarantee with real-time email verification $99 to $199 a month ($74 and $149 annual) 8. Lusha Self-serve simplicity Fast individual lookups, free 40 credits a month Free; Pro around $29 to $52, Premium around $300/user/month 9. Kaspr EU solo sellers and small businesses Browser-extension prospecting for European contacts Free, €45, or €79 a month 10. Seamless.AI High-volume US list building Real-time search claiming over 1.3 billion records (vendor figure) Free published; Pro and Enterprise gated Pricing per each vendor's public pricing page or, where gated, per published buyer reports. How we chose We ranked on five criteria: coverage (contacts, companies, phones, regions), tested accuracy versus claimed accuracy, compliance posture (GDPR, CCPA, DNC handling), pricing transparency, and activation, meaning whether the data can actually be put to work without stitching more tools together. Every negative claim is attributed to its source. There is one more bias to disclose beyond our own: nearly every "best B2B data" list you will read is written by a vendor that ranks itself first. So is this one. The difference we aim for is that every other entry receives an honest verdict, a real strength, and a named reason to choose it over us. The 10 best B2B data providers in 2026 1. Artisan: Best for data plus activation in one platform Most data providers sell you a database and wish you luck with the rest of the stack you need to use it. Artisan builds the data layer directly into an AI BDR. Ava, Artisan's AI BDR, sources leads from a database of over 250 million B2B professionals across over 200 countries plus Artisan Local Data, which holds over 250 million local businesses (restaurants, gyms, local services), then enriches them through a waterfall that queries roughly a dozen providers in sequence. Emails are validated with bounce tests, and phone enrichment is only charged when a number is actually found. The same platform layers on intent signals (funding rounds, hiring, tech-stack intent, website visitors) and then writes, sends, and answers the outreach itself across email, social media, and dialer call steps. Artisan Local Data is a real differentiator. SumUp used Artisan to reach local businesses that were previously out of reach, at a $52 cost per lead, generating 8 to 15 positive replies per week across hundreds of thousands of emails. Bruno Didier, CEO of CookUnity Business, puts the activation point plainly: "Ava runs highly targeted outreach at a scale we could never reach with a human-only team." CookUnity's cost per lead runs about $45. CRM depth matters for a data purchase, and Artisan syncs natively with Salesforce and HubSpot: full backfill import, a deduplication waterfall on import, field-level export control (do not sync, fill if empty, or overwrite), and CRM-driven do-not-contact rules. The deployment model scales up as well as down. On Enterprise plans, sales ops runs Ava centrally for large account executive (AE) teams who never log into the platform, with governance to match: plain-language escalation rules, an audit trail, org-level do-not-contact enforcement, and the field-level CRM controls above. Security posture includes SOC 2 Type II, GDPR and CCPA compliance, and SSO, and Enterprise plans add a forward-deployed strategist and a dedicated CSM. Best for: teams from founder-led startups on self-serve to enterprises running Ava centrally from sales ops, and any B2B team that wants one system for data, enrichment, signals, and outbound instead of paying for a database and then stitching together a sequencer, dialer, and enrichment tool to use it. Who should pick something else: teams that only want raw data, whether a licensed database or a lookup API feeding their own warehouse, should look at People Data Labs or ZoomInfo. Artisan's data is consumed through the platform, not sold as a standalone feed. Pricing: hybrid. Ava's work runs on usage-based credits, so you pay for the work she performs, and dialer seats and phone numbers are billed separately, with the dialer at $75/seat/month on monthly billing. Ava can be trialled for free. Details at artisan.co/pricing . 2. ZoomInfo: Best for enterprise US depth ZoomInfo (Nasdaq: $GTM since May 2025) remains the deepest US enterprise database: over 321 million professional profiles, over 174 million emails, and over 70 million direct dials, per its own published figures. Org charts, technographics, Scoops, and WebSights visitor identification round out a broad platform, and its Copilot Workspace (2026) adds an AI layer on top. For US enterprise account coverage, especially direct dials into large organizations, it is still the reference point. The limits are mostly commercial. Entry pricing typically starts around $15,000 a year and commonly runs $15,000 to $40,000, per published buyer reports, and the company is widely noted for aggressive contract and renewal terms. Its intent data is largely Bombora-derived, per multiple third-party comparisons, so you are partly paying a premium to access a co-op others also resell. And it is a data platform first. Outbound execution is an add-on, not the product. For a direct comparison, see Artisan vs. ZoomInfo . Best for: enterprises that need maximum US depth, org charts, and direct-dial coverage, and have the budget and procurement muscle to negotiate. Who should pick something else: small and medium-sized businesses (SMBs) and startups. The entry price is the product's own filter. EMEA-first teams receive better regional coverage and compliance tooling from Cognism. Pricing: quote-based, from around $15K a year per published buyer reports. 3. Apollo: Best price-performance Apollo pairs a database of over 230 million contacts with a full engagement platform (sequences, a dialer, and now AI features following its March 2026 acquisition of Pocus) at a price that starts at free and tops out at $119/user/month on public plans. Roughly 600,000 companies use it (around 100,000 paying), and it reportedly passed $200 million in annual recurring revenue (ARR), adoption and traction few vendors in the category can match. It has real limits, though. It is a single-source database, not a waterfall, so coverage gaps show up on hard-to-find contacts and mobile numbers. Per-seat pricing plus credit caps ("unlimited" email credits are fair-use limited around 10,000 a month) make heavy usage less cheap than it looks. And the AI is assistive: humans still run the motion. For head-to-head detail, see Artisan vs. Apollo , Apollo vs. Lusha , and Apollo vs. Outreach . Best for: startups, SMBs, and mid-market teams that want the best data-per-dollar ratio in the category with engagement built in. Who should pick something else: teams whose ideal customer profile (ICP) demands maximum phone coverage or EMEA compliance depth. A waterfall approach or Cognism will outperform a single source there. Pricing: free to $119/user/month, per apollo.io/pricing. 4. Cognism: Best for EMEA coverage and compliance Cognism is the compliance-first leader for European data. Its Diamond Data product ships phone-verified mobile numbers (the company claims up to 3x higher connect rates on verified mobiles), and it scrubs against DNC and Telephone Preference Service (TPS) registries across multiple markets, something almost no US-first rival does. ISO 27001, ISO 27701, and SOC 2 attestations back the positioning, and its Sales Companion product (January 2025) added a per-seller AI layer. Pricing is the main friction. It is fully gated, reported contracts run roughly $15,000 to $50,000 a year, real quotes commonly start around $20,000, and US depth trails ZoomInfo. There is also an awkward footnote covered below: Cognism owns Kaspr, which was fined by the French regulator in December 2024. Best for: mid-market and enterprise teams selling into Europe who need verified mobiles and defensible GDPR posture. Who should pick something else: US-only SMBs, who would pay a compliance premium for protections their market does not require. Pricing: quote-based, around $15K to $50K a year per published buyer reports. 5. Clay: Best for DIY waterfall orchestration Clay is not a database. It is the workbench that made waterfall enrichment famous: it connects over 150 enrichment providers into sequential lookups, adds AI research agents (Claygent, with over 1.5 billion tasks claimed), and lets a skilled operator build almost any data workflow. It raised $100 million at a $3.1 billion valuation (CapitalG, August 2025) and anchors the go-to-market (GTM) engineering movement. Keep in mind what Clay is not, though. It is infrastructure, not an outbound engine. It needs a skilled operator (the median "GTM engineer" posting pays around $160,000), and provider credits stack on top of the platform tiers (Launch from $167 a month, Growth from $446 a month), with median contracts around $30,000 a year per published contract data. It enriches. It does not send, call, or book. For a direct comparison, see Artisan vs. Clay . Best for: revenue operations and growth teams with a dedicated operator who want maximum control over multi-provider enrichment logic. Who should pick something else: teams without a GTM engineer. If you want waterfall coverage without building the waterfall, Artisan runs one internally, and budget point-solutions like FullEnrich ($55 a month per 1,000 credits) cover simple use cases. Pricing: free tier; Launch from $167 a month, Growth from $446 a month, per clay.com/pricing. 6. People Data Labs: Best API for developers and data teams People Data Labs licenses raw data instead of selling seats: an API over more than 3 billion person records (a vendor figure that includes historical and shallow profiles), used to power other products, enrich warehouses, and build internal tools. Pricing is unusually transparent for the category, with 100 free lookups and Pro from $98 a month (roughly $0.28 per lookup, falling to around $0.01 at bulk volume), and SOC 2 and ISO attestations cover the pipeline. Just know there is no application layer: no UI for sellers, no verification workflow, no outreach. Record freshness also varies widely across that headline figure of 3 billion, so treat it as a coverage ceiling, not a quality claim. Best for: engineering and data teams building enrichment into their own product or warehouse. Who should pick something else: sales teams that need a tool reps can actually use. This is a data feed, not a prospecting product. Pricing: free 100 lookups; Pro from $98 a month, per peopledatalabs.com. 7. UpLead: Best small-business option for verified accuracy UpLead's whole pitch is its 95% accuracy guarantee, backed by real-time email verification at export. You do not pay for records that fail. The database is smaller, at over 160 million contacts, but for SMB teams the trade of breadth for verified quality is often correct, and pricing is public: $99 a month Essentials and $199 a month Plus, dropping to $74 and $149 on annual billing. Coverage depth trails the big platforms, especially on mobile numbers and outside the US, and there is no engagement layer. Best for: startups and SMBs that would rather have fewer, verified contacts than a bigger, noisier database. Who should pick something else: enterprise teams that need org charts, intent, and integrations depth. That is ZoomInfo or Cognism territory. Pricing: $99 to $199 a month ($74 and $149 annual), per uplead.com/pricing. 8. Lusha: Best for self-serve individual lookups Lusha made its name on frictionless self-serve prospecting: sign up free, receive 40 credits a month, and look up contacts one at a time or in small lists. Paid plans run roughly $29 to $52/user/month on Pro, while Premium now runs around $300/user/month on a credit slider. For an individual seller or a two-person team that needs occasional lookups, the simplicity is the feature. A recurring complaint theme among users, the "credit trap," concerns annual plans front-loading credits that expire. Accuracy on mobiles is inconsistent outside core markets. Best for: individual contributors and very small teams doing low-volume, ad-hoc prospecting. Who should pick something else: any team doing systematic outbound. Per-credit economics and coverage both degrade at volume. Pricing: free; Pro around $29 to $52/user/month, Premium around $300/user/month, per lusha.com/pricing. 9. Kaspr: Best for EU solo sellers, with a compliance asterisk Kaspr, owned by Cognism, is a browser-extension prospecting tool aimed at European SMBs and individual sellers: free tier, then €45 and €79 monthly plans, with credits for emails and phones pulled as you browse professional profiles. As a cheap on-ramp to European contact data, it works. The asterisk is significant. France's data regulator CNIL fined Kaspr €240,000 in December 2024 for GDPR violations related to its data collection, which matters given the parent company's compliance-first marketing. Best for: European freelancers and small teams that need cheap, occasional contact lookups. Who should pick something else: anyone whose legal team reads regulator decisions. Mid-market and up should buy the parent (Cognism) or a waterfall approach instead. Pricing: free, €45, or €79 a month, per kaspr.io/pricing. 10. Seamless.AI: Highest claimed volume, buyer beware Seamless.AI positions itself as a real-time search engine over a claimed 1.3 billion records with roughly 98% accuracy. For pure US list-building volume, users report it finds contacts other tools miss. The caution flags are unusually loud. Users report bounce rates of 20% to 30% on exported lists, far from the claimed 98% accuracy. Contracts are annual-only with a reported 60- to 90-day auto-renewal notice window, a recurring complaint theme among buyers. And in March 2025, the company saw the reported removal of its company page from a major professional network over scraping practices, as covered in industry reporting at the time. Best for: high-volume US list builders who will verify every export through a separate validation step and read the contract terms twice. Who should pick something else: anyone who cannot absorb verification overhead or auto-renewal risk. UpLead or Apollo deliver calmer economics. Pricing: only the Free plan is published now; Pro and Enterprise are gated (contact sales), annual-only. Should you buy a static database or use waterfall enrichment? Waterfall enrichment beats a static database for most teams in 2026. A static database is one vendor's snapshot: you inherit their coverage, their gaps, and their decay rate. A waterfall queries multiple providers in sequence. If provider one has no mobile number, provider two is asked, then provider three, which adds roughly 20% to 40% coverage versus any single source. The shift to waterfalls was the defining change in this category between 2024 and 2026. The trade-off is operational. Running your own waterfall through Clay gives maximum control but requires an operator and stacked provider credits. Buying a single database is simple but caps your coverage at one vendor's reach. A third path is a product with the waterfall built in. Artisan, for example, runs enrichment across roughly a dozen providers internally, validates emails with bounce tests, and charges for phone numbers only on success, so you receive the coverage of a waterfall without the assembly work. Budget standalone waterfalls (FullEnrich, BetterContact) cover the middle ground for teams that just need enrichment. For a wider roundup, see the best B2B data enrichment tools . Which B2B data provider has the most accurate contact data? No provider's headline accuracy claim survives contact with reality, so the real answer is the most accurate setup, not the most accurate vendor. Vendor claims cluster at 95% or better. Independent-style testing consistently lands lower, roughly 65% to 90% for emails and 45% to 70% for phone numbers, and B2B contact data decays at roughly 20% to 30% a year as people change jobs. One more caveat is worth stating: essentially every published head-to-head benchmark in this category was run by a vendor, so treat all of them, including claims repeated in this article, as directional. What actually moves accuracy is verification at the point of use (UpLead's export-time verification, Artisan's bounce-testing before send), phone-verified sourcing (Cognism's Diamond Data), and waterfall redundancy, which lets a second provider correct the first one's stale record. If a vendor quotes one accuracy number for their whole database, ask how it was measured and when. Which provider has the best mobile phone number coverage? Cognism has the strongest single-vendor claim on mobiles. Diamond Data numbers are human- and phone-verified, the company claims up to 3x higher connect rates on them, and coverage is strongest in EMEA. ZoomInfo's 70 million direct dials (vendor figure) lead for US enterprise desk lines and mobiles. But because phone data is the weakest layer at every provider (independent-style tests put phone accuracy at just 45% to 70%), waterfall approaches tend to beat any single vendor on total mobile coverage. That logic is why Artisan charges for phone enrichment only when the waterfall actually returns a number, and why phones cost roughly 10x email credits at nearly every provider: scarce, decaying, and expensive to verify. For tools focused on contact details, see the best email and phone number finder tools for sales . How compliant is your B2B data provider? Compliance became a real buying axis in 2025 and 2026, not a checkbox. The spread within a single corporate family shows how uneven the category is. Cognism markets DNC and TPS scrubbing across markets and holds ISO 27001, ISO 27701, and SOC 2 attestations, while its own subsidiary Kaspr was fined €240,000 by CNIL, France's data regulator, in December 2024 for GDPR violations. Meanwhile, Seamless.AI saw the reported removal of its company page from a major professional network over scraping practices (March 2025), per industry reporting. A few questions separate vendors quickly. Where is the data sourced, and is there a lawful basis under GDPR? Are DNC registries scrubbed before phone records reach reps? How are deletion requests handled downstream? If your outreach platform sits on top of the data, its handling matters too. Artisan, for instance, applies suppression lists before enrichment and enforces federal DNC checks on its dialer. For teams whose security reviews extend to the outbound stack itself, see our roundup of the best AI sales development representative (SDR) tools . What changed in the B2B data market in 2025 and 2026? Clearbit disappeared as a standalone product. HubSpot acquired it in December 2023, it was sunset through 2025, and it now lives on only as HubSpot Breeze Intelligence (around $45 a month per 100 credits inside HubSpot), with no phones and no standalone API. ZoomInfo repositioned around go-to-market. It changed its Nasdaq ticker to $GTM in May 2025 and shipped Copilot Workspace in 2026, repositioning from database to a go-to-market intelligence platform. Apollo bought Pocus on March 19, 2026, pushing toward an "AI-native GTM OS" on top of its data layer, with roughly $200 million ARR reported. The Kaspr fine landed (€240,000, CNIL, December 2024), the category's clearest regulatory shot across the bow, per the CNIL's published decision. Seamless.AI's professional-network removal was reported in March 2025, sharpening scrutiny of scraped-data sourcing across the category. Waterfall enrichment became table stakes, with dedicated tools (FullEnrich, BetterContact) and platforms with built-in waterfalls (Artisan) normalizing multi-provider enrichment. FAQ What is the best B2B data provider for startups and SMBs? Apollo for pure data-per-dollar (free to $119/user/month, over 230 million contacts), UpLead if you value verified accuracy over volume ($74 to $149 a month on annual billing). If you want the data already attached to an outbound engine so you skip buying a sequencer and enrichment tool separately, Artisan's hybrid model charges credits for the work Ava performs, with dialer seats billed separately, so you are not buying a seat for every rep who needs data. For a small team, that is often the simpler total-cost story. What is the best B2B data provider for enterprise sales teams? ZoomInfo for US-centric enterprises that need maximum depth, org charts, and direct dials, with typical contracts of $15,000 to $40,000 a year per published buyer reports. Cognism for enterprises selling into EMEA, where DNC scrubbing and phone-verified mobiles matter more than raw US volume. Many enterprises now pair one of these with a waterfall layer, since even the deepest single source misses 20% to 40% of what multi-provider lookups find. Artisan covers that pairing in one contract: waterfall enrichment plus an AI BDR that sales ops runs centrally for large AE teams, with SOC 2 Type II, SSO, and a dedicated CSM on Enterprise plans. Which tool combines B2B data, enrichment, and automated outreach? Artisan is built specifically for this: over 250 million B2B professionals across over 200 countries, Artisan Local Data with over 250 million local businesses, waterfall enrichment across roughly a dozen providers, intent signals, and an AI BDR (Ava) who writes, sends, and answers outreach across email, social media, and dialer call steps in one system instead of a stitched stack. Apollo also bundles data with engagement, though humans still run the motion. Clay orchestrates data brilliantly but hands off the outreach to other tools. See our companion guide to the best AI sales tools . What is the best data enrichment tool for Salesforce? ZoomInfo has the most mature native Salesforce enrichment app for keeping CRM fields current at enterprise scale. Clay is strongest for custom enrichment logic pushed into Salesforce. Artisan approaches it from the activation side: full Salesforce backfill import, a deduplication waterfall, field-level export control (do not sync, fill if empty, or overwrite), and CRM-driven do-not-contact. That is enrichment in service of outbound instead of field hygiene alone. Which B2B data provider has the most accurate contact data? Treat every accuracy claim skeptically: vendors advertise 95% or better, independent-style tests find 65% to 90% for emails and 45% to 70% for phones, and data decays 20% to 30% annually. The practically accurate options are those that verify at the point of use. UpLead verifies emails at export, Cognism phone-verifies Diamond Data mobiles, and Artisan bounce-tests emails and charges for phones only on success. Waterfall setups beat any single vendor by cross-checking sources. Is a free B2B database worth using? Free tiers are real but narrow. Apollo's free plan is the most generous real database access; Lusha gives 40 credits a month; UpLead and most others offer trials. Free tiers work for validating that a vendor covers your ICP before buying. They do not work for running actual outbound volume. Credit ceilings and missing phone data are the point at which every vendor converts you. How much does B2B data cost in 2026? The spread is enormous: free (Apollo, Lusha, and Seamless.AI all publish free tiers) to $99 to $199 a month (UpLead), roughly $29 to $300/user/month (Lusha Pro to Premium), $167 to $446 a month plus provider credits (Clay's Launch and Growth tiers), and $15,000 to $50,000 a year for enterprise contracts (ZoomInfo, Cognism), per each vendor's pricing page or published buyer reports. Two rules hold consistently: phone numbers cost roughly 10x email credits, and gated pricing usually signals a four- to five-figure annual contract. What happened to Clearbit? Clearbit no longer exists as a standalone product. HubSpot acquired it in December 2023 and sunset the standalone offering through 2025; the technology now powers HubSpot Breeze Intelligence at roughly $45 a month per 100 credits, inside HubSpot only, with no phone numbers and no standalone API. Former Clearbit users typically migrate to Apollo or People Data Labs (API use cases), or to platforms with built-in enrichment such as Artisan. Put the data to work A database is only as good as the pipeline it produces. Artisan pairs the data layer (over 250 million B2B professionals, over 250 million local businesses, waterfall enrichment, intent signals) with Ava, an AI BDR who turns records into meetings. Start a free trial or see how pricing works : Ava's work runs on usage-based credits, so you pay for the work she performs, with dialer seats billed separately.
